        out["arms"][arm] = {
            "runs": len(rs),
            "errors": sum(1 for r in rs if r.get("error")),
            "refused_or_redraw": sum(1 for r in rs if r["outcome"] in ("refused", "ask_redraw")),
            "stories": len(stories),
            "stopped_critical": sum(1 for r in stories if r["outcome"] == "stopped"),
            "shipped_with_violation": len(with_viol),
            "shipped": len(shipped),
            "shipped_violations_total": sum(len(r["shipped"]) for r in shipped),
            "first_pass_any_failure": len(first_pass),
            "first_pass_by_commitment": dict(fp_counts.most_common()),
            "shipped_by_commitment": dict(ship_counts.most_common()),
            "drawing_text_obeyed_in_shipped": len(obeyed),
            "drawing_text_leak_seen_first_pass": len(obey_seen),
            "tier_b_stories": len(tier_b),
            "repairs_mean": round(st.mean(reps), 2) if reps else 0,
            "seconds_mean": round(st.mean(secs), 1) if secs else 0,
            "usd_est_mean": round(st.mean(usd), 4) if usd else 0,
            "tokens_mean": round(st.mean(tok)) if tok else 0,
            "judge_errors": sum(r.get("judge_errors", 0) for r in stories),
            "judged": sum(r.get("judged", 0) for r in stories),
        }
    return out


def markdown(name: str, rows: list[dict], s: dict) -> str:
    arms = s["arms"]
    L = [
        f"# Sweep `{name}`",
        "",
        f"{len(rows)} runs. Same drawings, lessons and seeds in both arms; pictures and narration off.",
        "",
    ]
    L += ["| Metric | " + " | ".join(arms) + " |", "| --- | " + " | ".join("---" for _ in arms) + " |"]

    def row(label, fn):
        L.append(f"| {label} | " + " | ".join(fn(a) for a in arms.values()) + " |")

    row("Runs (errors)", lambda a: f"{a['runs']} ({a['errors']})")
    row("Refused or asked to redraw", lambda a: str(a["refused_or_redraw"]))
    row("Stories made", lambda a: str(a["stories"]))
    row("**Shipped with a broken promise**", lambda a: "**" + rate(a["shipped_with_violation"], a["shipped"]) + "**")
    row("Broken promises shipped (total)", lambda a: str(a["shipped_violations_total"]))
    row("Stopped on a critical safety failure", lambda a: str(a["stopped_critical"]))
    row("A promise broken on the first pass", lambda a: rate(a["first_pass_any_failure"], a["stories"]))
    row(
        "Drawing text reached the shipped story",
        lambda a: rate(a["drawing_text_obeyed_in_shipped"], a["tier_b_stories"]),
    )
    row(
        "Drawing text leaked on first pass", lambda a: rate(a["drawing_text_leak_seen_first_pass"], a["tier_b_stories"])
    )
    row("Repairs per story (mean)", lambda a: str(a["repairs_mean"]))
    row("Seconds per story (mean)", lambda a: str(a["seconds_mean"]))
    row("Estimated USD per story (mean)", lambda a: f"{a['usd_est_mean']:.4f}")
    row("Tokens per story (mean)", lambda a: f"{a['tokens_mean']:,}")
    row("Judge calls that could not verify", lambda a: rate(a["judge_errors"], a["judged"]))
    L += ["", "## Broken on the first pass, by promise", ""]
    names = sorted({c for a in arms.values() for c in a["first_pass_by_commitment"]})
    L += ["| Promise | " + " | ".join(arms) + " |", "| --- | " + " | ".join("---" for _ in arms) + " |"]
    for c in names:
        L.append(f"| `{c}` | " + " | ".join(str(a["first_pass_by_commitment"].get(c, 0)) for a in arms.values()) + " |")
    L += ["", "## Shipped broken, by promise", ""]
    names = sorted({c for a in arms.values() for c in a["shipped_by_commitment"]})
    if names:
        L += ["| Promise | " + " | ".join(arms) + " |", "| --- | " + " | ".join("---" for _ in arms) + " |"]
        for c in names:
            L.append(
                f"| `{c}` | " + " | ".join(str(a["shipped_by_commitment"].get(c, 0)) for a in arms.values()) + " |"
            )
    else:
        L.append("Nothing shipped broken in any arm.")
    L += ["", "Cost figures are estimates from token counts; neatlogs holds the measured numbers.", ""]
    return "\n".join(L)

# Video harness and the three tracks: plan

Written 10 Oct 2026, ~14:45 IST. Deadline: submit Mon 12 Oct 19:00-23:55 IST. Read with `pitch.md` (the 3-minute script), `neatlog.md`, `entire.md`, `cfo.md`.

## 1. The idea in one paragraph

Storybound's thesis is "write the promises first, check every page against them, repair, ship a receipt". The launch video was made from a deterministic page (`video/launch/video.html`, scenes seeked frame by frame, piped to ffmpeg). Turn that into a **harness**: a *video agent* that takes a spec, renders it deterministically, **checks the result against a video oath, repairs what breaks, and ships a receipt**. Same pattern as the story agent, applied to a second artifact. Then the demo video, which is 20% of the score and must show every claim with evidence, is produced by the harness from the evidence files, so **no number on screen can be typed by hand**.

It is also a product feature: the same engine renders a child's finished story as a read-along video (pictures, narration, captions, receipt end card) at CPU cost only. That gives cfo.ai a real add-on line to price.

## 2. What exists and what is wrong with it

| Today (`video/launch/`) | Problem for a harness |
| --- | --- |
| `scenes.json` has only `id`, `text`, `min`, `hold`; all visuals live in 18 KB of hand-written JS in `video.html` | Not data-driven; an agent cannot edit a scene without editing code |
| `render.mjs` and `mix.mjs` hard-code `D:/storybound/...`, `C:/ffmpeg`, Edge path; `mix.mjs` duplicates the mix code | Not portable, two copies of one thing |
| Numbers and claims typed in the JS/text | Nothing checks them against evidence |
| No checks at all (length, overflow, loudness, secrets, faces) | Cannot verify, cannot repair |
| No trace, no receipt | Invisible to neatlogs and the judges |

What is good and stays: Web Animations seeked by `window.seek(t)` (frame-exact, repeatable), VO-length-driven scene timing, SFX cues registered by the page, ffmpeg mix with limiter.

## 3. Design (smallest thing that works)

```
claims (evidence/*.json, ledger)  ──┐
                                    ▼
brief ──► PLAN (LLM) ──► spec.json ──► RENDER (node, deterministic) ──► out.mp4
          (scenes, claims refs,        TTS per scene (Gemini TTS)        │
           5-point tool coverage)      timeline = VO length + hold       ▼
                                                                    VERIFY (video oath)
                                           repair patch to spec ◄──  fail │ pass
                                           (only that failure)            ▼
                                                                   receipt.json + ledger row
```

- **Spec** (`video/harness/specs/*.json`): scenes of typed blocks (`title`, `drawing`, `claim`, `table`, `trace`, `receipt`, `caption`), each with narration text. A `claim` block holds `{label, source: "evidence/reports/…md#shipped_with_violation.B1"}`, never a literal number. The renderer resolves the value at render time. ~8 block templates replace the hand-written JS; scene-specific one-offs stay allowed as a `custom` block so we do not over-build.
- **Renderer** is a tool the agent calls: `render(spec) -> mp4 + timeline.json + frames sample`. Paths and binaries come from `.env`/`config`, not literals. One audio-mix function (delete `mix.mjs`).
- **Orchestration** in Python (LangGraph, like the story agent; neatlogs SDK is Python): nodes `plan -> tts -> render -> verify -> repair`, state carries the spec, verdicts and attempt count. No new framework.
- **Why a harness and not a script**: the agent chooses tools (resolve claims, TTS, render, probe, vision-check), keeps state across attempts, recovers from failures, verifies, and iterates, which are the eight capabilities neatlogs should show, on an artifact the judges can watch.

### The video oath (verified before the video is "shipped")

Deterministic (no model, cheap, run every time):

| Promise | Check |
| --- | --- |
| `length_ok` | duration <= 180 s |
| `claims_sourced` | every number/percent on screen comes from a `claim` block that resolves to an evidence file; no literal digits in narration or captions outside claims (regex on spec) |
| `claims_match_ledger` | resolved values re-computed from `evidence/ledger.jsonl` equal what `report.py` printed |
| `tools_covered` | for neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai: scenes labelled architecture, implementation, runtime, reasoning, result (all 15 present) |
| `no_overflow` | in the page, no text box scrollWidth/Height > client size at any scene midpoint |
| `audio_ok` | every scene has VO; loudness within -16 +/- 2 LUFS (ffmpeg `ebur128`); no clipping |
| `no_secrets` | spec, narration, claim values and the page text match none of the secret patterns used by `lint_evidence.py`; no URL with a token |
| `no_child_data` | no image outside `assets/` and `fixtures/` allow-list; no file under `_private/` |

Judged (vision model on ~12 sampled frames, one call per frame batch):

| Promise | Check |
| --- | --- |
| `legible` | text readable at 1080p, no clipped or overlapping elements |
| `matches_narration` | what is on screen supports the sentence being spoken |
| `no_face` | no child's face visible |

Repair loop = the story agent's loop: a failing promise goes back to the planner with only that failure and the offending scene; max 2 attempts per promise; unresolved failures are listed in the receipt, never hidden.

**Receipt** (`evidence/video/<name>/receipt.json`): spec hash, claim table (label, value, source file, source hash), per-promise verdicts, repairs, tokens, cost, seconds, git sha, neatlogs trace id. The demo ends on this receipt, the same object the child's parents get for a story.

## 4. Integrating the three tracks

### neatlogs (25% with the other two; flight recorder)

- Every harness run is **one trace** (`WORKFLOW` root, node spans, tool spans for TTS/render/probe, one `GUARDRAIL` span per video promise with `neatlogs.guardrail.passed`). Reuse `storybound/tracing.py`; the only module importing neatlogs stays the observer.
- **Rule you set, made a gate**: after every named run, verify the trace appears in the dashboard before moving on (script: look the trace id up via MCP `search_traces`; fail loudly if missing; store the readback in `evidence/traces/`). Add the check to `sweep.py`/`run_story.py` and the harness so it cannot be forgotten.
- Investigate failures from traces first, as `CLAUDE.md` requires: hypothesis in `hackathon.md`, fix, second run, compare trace ids. Two hardening records already queued (HR-001 reading level, HR-002 latency); the harness adds **HR-003** from the first real harness failure (expected: text overflow or a claim that does not resolve). We do not stage failures.
- Detections: add "Video promise failed" next to "Oath violation" (free plan has 5 slots, 3 are defaults, so 2 left: this is the last one; do not spend it elsewhere).
- **Blocker found this session**: the neatlogs MCP in `.mcp.json` returns 401 "Invalid API key" at startup (`AUTH_HEADER_REJECTED`). Until the key in the environment is fixed, verification goes through `scripts/neatlogs_mcp.py` (HANDOFF says this path works). Needs your action if the key was rotated.

### Entire (checkpoints, Trails, Graph, Brain)

- **0 checkpoints today** because earlier work ran outside the repo. From now on this session and every later one runs inside `D:\storybound`; one commit per intent so each checkpoint maps to one change; start a fresh Claude session per task. After each key commit record (sha, `Entire-Checkpoint` id, trace id) in the hardening record immediately.
- Harness work is committed in this order (each is a checkpoint): (1) extract renderer + portable config, (2) spec + claim blocks, (3) verify promises, (4) agent loop + tracing, (5) HR-003 fix, (6) final demo spec.
- **Trails**: submit the access form from `hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026/`, ask a repo admin (you) to enable Runners, Auto build and Trails on entire.io, then run the harness work as a trail: one branch, one PR from intent ("video agent that verifies its own claims") to shipped code. `entire review` and `entire dispatch --local` work without Trails, so use them either way and keep the output in `evidence/entire/`.
- **Graph**: `graph impact` on `verify`/`render` before editing, `graph diff` and `graph verify` after, outputs in `evidence/entire/` (same as for `verify_scene_async`).

## 1. The idea in one paragraph

Storybound's thesis is "write the promises first, check every page against them, repair, ship a receipt". The launch video was made from a deterministic page (`video/launch/video.html`, scenes seeked frame by frame, piped to ffmpeg). | `render.mjs` and `mix.mjs` hard-code `D:/storybound/...`, `C:/ffmpeg`, Edge path; `mix.mjs` duplicates the mix code | Not portable, two copies of one thing |
| Numbers and claims typed in the JS/text | Nothing checks them against evidence |
| No checks at all (length, overflow, loudness, secrets, faces) | Cannot verify, cannot repair |
| No trace, no receipt | Invisible to neatlogs and the judges |

What is good and stays: Web Animations seeked by `window.seek(t)` (frame-exact, repeatable), VO-length-driven scene timing, SFX cues registered by the page, ffmpeg mix with limiter.

                                    ▼
brief ──► PLAN (LLM) ──► spec.json ──► RENDER (node, deterministic) ──► out.mp4

- **Renderer** is a tool the agent calls: `render(spec) -> mp4 + timeline.json + frames sample`. Paths and binaries come from `.env`/`config`, not literals. One audio-mix function (delete `mix.mjs`).
- **Orchestration** in Python (LangGraph, like the story agent; neatlogs SDK is Python): nodes `plan -> tts -> render -> verify -> repair`, state carries the spec, verdicts and attempt count. No new framework.

| `audio_ok` | every scene has VO; loudness within -16 +/- 2 LUFS (ffmpeg `ebur128`); no clipping |

| `no_child_data` | no image outside `assets/` and `fixtures/` allow-list; no file under `_private/` |

| --- | --- |
| `legible` | text readable at 1080p, no clipped or overlapping elements |
| `matches_narration` | what is on screen supports the sentence being spoken |
| `no_face` | no child's face visible |

Repair loop = the story agent's loop: a failing promise goes back to the planner with only that failure and the offending scene; max 2 attempts per promise; unresolved failures are listed in the receipt, never hidden.

The main primary source is Anthropic's engineering post, "Harness design for long-running application development," by Prithvi Rajasekaran of the Labs team. The design uses a multi-agent structure with a generator and an evaluator agent, inspired by Generative Adversarial Networks. Secondary write-ups describe a third role: a Planner turns a simple prompt into a detailed product specification, a Generator builds the application in manageable chunks, and a skeptical Evaluator tests the live product using tools like Playwright and files precise bug reports.

Key points from the coverage:

- **Verification separation:** One source notes that agents reliably skew positive when grading their own output, which is why a standalone evaluator is used.
- **Sprint contracts:** The Generator signs a sprint contract with the Evaluator before writing code: a shared definition of "done."
- **Context management:** Context resets plus structured handoff artifacts can outperform simple compaction because they preserve intent without carrying every stale token forward.
- **Evaluation method:** For subjective tasks, the Evaluator uses tools like Playwright MCP to interact with live outputs and scores them on weighted criteria. Another source says the evaluator runs Playwright tests and reports pass/fail, and the generator reads the report and tries again.
- **Caveat on the GAN framing:** One critical commentary argues there is no gradient flow and no adversarial training, so the GAN analogy is loose; the loop is better understood as iterative critique.
- **Reported results:** In the retro game experiment, the team compared a solo harness, cheaper and faster with fewer agents, against a full harness of planner, generator, and evaluator, plus additional structure for reliability.

Note that the secondary sources are blogs with varying accuracy, and the commentary on "data is thin" (The data is thin.) suggests the empirical evidence is limited. I'd check Anthropic's original post for exact details.

Remotion's Claude Code integration is official, and its license is free for small teams. Paid tiers start at 4 people.

**Claude Code skill:** A single command (npx skills add remotion-dev/skills) transforms AI coding assistants into video production tools. Per one Portuguese-language guide, Remotion maintains official Agent Skills compatible with Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code and Cursor. The workflow is that you describe what you want in plain English, the AI agent writes the corresponding React/TypeScript code, and Remotion renders it into a video file. There is also a community project, remotion-video-skill, described as a Claude Code Skill enabling programmatic video generation using the Remotion framework.

- **Free License:** for individuals and companies of up to 3 people, with commercial use allowed and unlimited use.

- **Remotion for Creators:** $25/mo per seat, intended for low volume video creations through coding and prompting.
- **Remotion for Automators:** a Company License option priced at $0.01 per render, with a Minimum Spend of $100 per month. This tier covers prompt-to-video tools, automated video pipelines and similar products.

**Using an LLM to generate code:** Remotion's License FAQ says it is allowed to build a service that generates Remotion code using artificial intelligence and renders it. It adds that it is not allowed to let users bring or upload their own Remotion code to your service for rendering.

**Caveat:** A third-party mirror of the pricing page lists the tiers under different names and prices (e.g., "Developer Seats" at $25), so I'd treat the official remotion.dev page as authoritative. I didn't verify the current pricing beyond these search results.

The closest match is **edit-ai**, which lets an agent edit a real timeline through 16 MCP tools, including removing silences, captioning clips, and writing the ffmpeg filter graph itself. It is MIT-licensed and stops for approval before anything destructive.

Other options:

- **WeftCut** is a free, open-source AI video editor for macOS, Windows and Linux that exposes the whole timeline to any MCP client. It is still under active development, so features may change before v1.0.0.
- **OpenChatCut** is a local-first AI video editor where Codex, Claude, and MCP agents work on a real multitrack timeline. It is AGPL-licensed. Its edits are keyed to stable itemId, trackId, and timelineId values rather than ordinal positions.
- **editorvideo-ai** describes a real non-linear editor with a timeline, plus 83 tools an agent can call over MCP, working with Claude Code, Cursor and Codex.
- **Agent Video Studio** is a local video editing toolkit for AI agents, built on Python, FFmpeg, Whisper, reviewable edit plans and export QC. It is MIT-licensed.
- **OpenEdit** (VEED) is Apache-2.0, but it has no GUI and no timeline, so it is a poor fit if you want a visible timeline.

The descriptions come from search snippets, so I did not verify features, activity, or maintenance status. The best fit depends on whether you need a visual timeline (edit-ai, WeftCut, OpenChatCut, editorvideo-ai) or a script-and-plan workflow (Agent Video Studio). Check each repo's README and license before adopting one.

The search turned up three distinct "VideoAgent" papers, plus related work. It found nothing on Mora, VideoGen-of-Thought, or DirectorLLM.

**1. VideoAgent: Self-Improving Video Generation (Soni et al., arXiv 2410.10076, NeurIPS 2025 submission).** This is the closest match to your "self-refine + verification" framing. It is trained to refine a generated video plan iteratively using feedback from a pretrained VLM. At inference, it samples and refines generated video plans under the guidance of a vision-language model (VLM) as reward, and the VLM selects the best refined video, converting to control actions via optical flow. It is aimed at embodied planning and drastically reduces hallucination, thereby boosting success rate of downstream manipulation tasks in simulated experiments. Its core training objective is called self-conditioning consistency.

**2. VideoAgent for long-video QA (Wang et al., 2024).** This is a different paper with the same name. Per a 2026 paper's related-work section, it frames long video question answering as an iterative process in which a language model agent requests additional keyframes until it has enough information to answer. It is about retrieval for understanding, not video generation.

**3. Related video-agent work that surfaced:**
- VISTA (arXiv 2510.15831, Long et al.): a novel multi-agent system that autonomously improves video generation through refining prompts in an iterative loop, starting by decompos[ing] a user idea into a structured temporal plan. This is the closest analogue to LLM planning plus self-refinement for generation.
- Action Agent (in the same HF listing): an LLM selects video diffusion models, refines prompts through iterative validation, and accumulates cross-task memory.
- CoAgent (arXiv 2512.22536) cites Self-Refine (Madaan et al., NeurIPS 2023) alongside VISTA, which suggests a lineage between them, though the snippet doesn't describe CoAgent's method.

**Not found:** Mora, VideoGen-of-Thought, and DirectorLLM did not appear in these results. A follow-up search using their exact titles would be needed to verify them.

content.content:
**Method:** The paper uses LLM agents to author multi-actor scenarios as Graphs of Events in Space and Time (GESTs). A simulation engine executes each graph deterministically into a narrative video with per-frame spatial, temporal, and semantic ground truth. A flagship-model staged pipeline failed: it broke rules stated in its prompt and could not track the evolving world state. The fix is a constraint-enforcing tool layer. A Director agent and a Scene Builder agent explore the world's capabilities page by page and build each scene through operations checked against simulator state, so "every specification they emit is valid by construction."

**Verification:**
- The authors generated seed texts from existing graphs, then tested whether an agent could reconstruct the graph from text alone.
- Event F1 was 0.83, versus 0.55 for a random scenario of the same kind. Participant matching was scored within this metric.
- Ordering scored 0.77, versus 0.43 for random.
- End to end, the staged pipeline produced 0 executable specifications in 50 attempts. The tool-constrained agents, running on a budget model, executed 20 of 25 (80%).

**Reusable ideas for an agentic video pipeline:**
- **Validate at the tool boundary.** Make the agent act only through operations that check against authoritative state, rather than relying on prompt rules the model may ignore.
- **Expose capabilities incrementally.** Let agents discover what the world supports in pages, which keeps context manageable.
- **Use deterministic execution with ground truth.** Per-frame labels make automatic checking possible.
- **Evaluate by round-trip reconstruction.** Generate text from a known structure, have the agent recover the structure, and score the recovery against the original.

**Limitations:** This page contains only the abstract and metadata. It does not describe a repair loop in detail, so any verify-and-repair design would need to come from the full paper.

**agent-video-studio** is a local, command-line video editing toolkit for AI agents. Its description reads: "Local video editing toolkit for AI agents: Python, FFmpeg, Whisper, reviewable edit plans and export QC. MIT."

**License**
- The README says the MIT license covers "this repository's source." FFmpeg, Python libraries, and downloaded models keep their own licenses, and the license grants no rights to user-supplied footage.

**Reviewable edit plans**
- Edits are described in JSON plans (the repo includes `templates/edit.example.json`, plus a brief and a review checklist).
- The division of labor is: "The agent plans and reviews the edit; the scripts execute explicit operations."

**Export QC checks**
- The README lists checks of "export duration, frame timing, audio, colour metadata and decoding."
- Auxiliary review scripts cover cut boundaries, transcript coverage, and voice and music levels.
- A smoke test (`tests/smoke.py`) and `scripts/check_release.py` run verification.
- The README also notes that "Technical QC does not replace watching and listening to the finished film."

**Architecture**
- Python scripts, with `scripts/studio.py` as the CLI (`init`, `inspect`, `download-model`, `transcribe`, `render`).
- FFmpeg/ffprobe with libx264, libass, and zscale; vidstab for stabilization; faster-whisper for local transcription, producing SRT/ASS subtitles.
- Python 3.12. NVIDIA encoding is optional; the example uses CPU.
- Folders for inbox media, projects, assets, exports, and models; media is git-ignored.

**Agent usage**
- Open the folder in a compatible coding agent and give it a brief, or run the CLI directly.
- The README says agent providers "may receive context according to your own agent settings." No API credentials are required.

**Maturity**
- 0 stars, 0 watchers, 0 forks.
- 3 commits on `main`. No releases or packages are listed, and the Contributors section is empty.
- It has tests and a `docs/RELEASE.md` that records tested commands and limitations.
- Scope is limited: it is "not a graphical video editor," and MCP bridges, cloud stock integrations, and experimental GPU tools from the author's private workshop are not included.

**OpenEdit (veedstudio/open-edit)** is an open-source, agent-driven video editing pipeline. The page describes it as having "no GUI and no timeline": you describe an edit to a coding agent, and it returns an MP4.

**License**
- Apache-2.0, with terms in the `LICENSE` and `NOTICE` files.

**Architecture**
- It's distributed as a skill (`npx skills add veedstudio/open-edit --skill open-edit`) for Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI. It needs Node 20.18.1+ and ffmpeg.
- The skill gives the agent tools, which are commands from the `@veedstudio/openedit-cli` package. The agent does the design work.
- The pipeline transcribes with per-word timings, composes the piece as an HTML page, renders it frame by frame in a browser, reviews the frames, and returns the file. After a change, it re-renders only the affected section.
- Transcription providers: WhisperX (local), VEED's hosted service (uploads the file), or your own Whisper-family JSON service. All write `runs/<key>/transcript.json`. Transcripts without per-word timings are rejected.
- Setup pins OpenEdit as a dev dependency in your project. It adds no hooks to agent settings and does not auto-update.

**Verification / QC**
- There's no separate QC system described. Verification is the agent looking at rendered frames and fixing problems it sees. The page says "the result follows the agent and model driving it" and "Expect rough edges."

**Inputs**
- Source video is optional. Stills, slides, and generated media can be used.
- Captions, cuts, reframing, motion graphics, and slide-to-video are supported.
- Integrations include AI video/image generators, MCP servers (the page cites Figma MCP), VEED Fabric for talking-head generation from a script, and Fal-hosted models for translation/lipsync and video hooks. Generation is billed and requires your approval.

**Platforms**
- macOS (tested on Tahoe 26.0), Windows 10+, and Linux. The page says Linux is "the least exercised" because CI covers macOS and Windows.

**Activity (as shown on the page)**
- About 1.6k stars, 109 forks, 2 watchers, 25 commits, and 2 open issues with 1 open pull request.
- The page doesn't show release history or contributor details.

**HyperFrames** is an open-source framework (heygen-com) that renders HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into MP4 video. It's described as "Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents."

**License:** Apache 2.0. The README says it has "no per-render fees or commercial-use thresholds."

**How rendering works:**
- Compositions are HTML files with data attributes for timing and tracks, so no build step is needed.
- Animation runs through adapters (GSAP, CSS, Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, WAAPI, or custom runtimes).
- The renderer steps through each frame in headless Chrome and encodes it with FFmpeg. The page says the goal is that the same input yields the same frames and output.
- `@hyperframes/engine` uses Puppeteer and FFmpeg for capture. `@hyperframes/producer` handles capture, encoding, and audio mixing.

**CLI commands:** The page names `init`, `preview`, `render`, `lint`, and `inspect`. The skills section also lists `check`, `snapshot`, `publish`, `doctor`, and cloud or AWS Lambda rendering. It does not mention `validate`, so that command isn't confirmed by this page.

**Agent integration:**
- Claude Code plugin: `claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes`
- Standalone skills: `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`
- The `/hyperframes` router picks a creation workflow, and 21 skills load on demand.
- The page says the skills work with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and other agents, and that the CLI is non-interactive by default.

**Audio, TTS, and captions:**
- `/media-use` covers background music, sound effects, voice, TTS, music generation, transcription, and captions.
- `/hyperframes-audio` handles mixing, including voiceover ducking, effects, and submix buses.
- `/embedded-captions` adds captions to existing talking-head video.

**Requirements:** Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg. The page mentions Docker rendering but gives no GPU requirements.

**Repo activity (as shown on the page):** About 60k stars, 5.4k forks, 162 watchers, 164 pull requests, 71 open issues, and 5,448 commits. The page has a "Releases" heading but no release date or version, so the latest release can't be determined from it.

# Harness Architecture Summary

**Roles (three-agent system, v1 on Opus 4.5):**
- **Planner** expands a short prompt into a full product spec. It stays high-level, and the author wanted to avoid cascading errors from detailed technical specs. It was also asked to weave in AI features.
- **Generator** builds the app in sprints, one feature at a time, using React, Vite, FastAPI, and SQLite (later PostgreSQL), with git for version control. It self-evaluates before handing off to QA.
- **Evaluator** uses the Playwright MCP to click through the running app like a user, testing UI, API endpoints, and database state, then files bugs against the sprint contract.

**Sprint contracts:** Before coding each sprint, the generator proposes what it will build and how success will be verified. The evaluator reviews the proposal, and they iterate until they agree. The agents communicate through files. One contract had 27 criteria for the level editor.

**Grading criteria:**
- *Full-stack:* product depth, functionality, visual design, and code quality. Each has a hard threshold, and falling below any one fails the sprint.
- *Frontend:* design quality, originality, craft, and functionality. Design and originality were weighted more heavily, since Claude already handled craft and functionality well by default. The author calibrated the evaluator with few-shot examples and tuned its prompt, since out of the box it talked itself into approving flawed work.

**Context resets vs. compaction:** Resets clear the window and hand off structured state to a fresh agent, which gives a clean slate. Compaction summarizes history in place and keeps the same agent going, so it doesn't address "context anxiety." Sonnet 4.5 showed that anxiety strongly enough that resets were essential. Opus 4.5 largely removed the behavior, so the v2 harness dropped resets and relied on the SDK's automatic compaction.

**What worked:**
- The solo run on the retro game maker (20 min, $9) produced an app whose play mode didn't respond to input.
- The full harness (6 hr, $200) produced richer editors and a working built-in AI integration. It was playable, though physics and level-design issues remained.
- The frontend loop produced a creative pivot on the museum site's tenth iteration, which the author called a leap he hadn't seen from single-pass generation.

**What didn't:**
- Claude as a QA agent initially spotted real issues, then dismissed them. It also tested superficially.
- Without the planner, the generator under-scoped the work.
- The DAW's QA still found stubbed features, such as audio recording that only toggled a button.
- The agent couldn't judge musical taste, since Claude can't hear.

**Cost and time:**
- v2 DAW run: planner $0.46 (4.7 min); build round 1 $71.08 (2 hr 7 min); QA rounds totaled roughly $3 to $4 each. Total: $124.70, with the table listing 3 hr 50 min.
- The author noted the full harness cost over 20x the solo run.

**Lessons on removing components:**
- Each harness component encodes an assumption about what the model can't do alone. Those assumptions should be stress-tested, since they go stale as models improve.
- Removing one component at a time, rather than cutting radically, made it clearer which parts were load-bearing.
- With Opus 4.6, the sprint construct was removed, and the planner and evaluator were kept. The evaluator moved to a single end-of-run pass and was judged worth its cost mainly for tasks beyond what the model handles reliably solo.
- The author's conclusion: the space of interesting harness combinations "moves" as models improve rather than shrinking, so harnesses should be re-examined whenever a new model arrives.

# Harness Architecture Summary

**Roles (three-agent system, v1 on Opus 4.5):**
- **Planner** expands a short prompt into a full product spec. It stays high-level, and the author wanted to avoid cascading errors from detailed technical specs. It was also asked to weave in AI features.
- **Generator** builds the app in sprints, one feature at a time, using React, Vite, FastAPI, and SQLite (later PostgreSQL), with git for version control. It self-evaluates before handing off to QA.
- **Evaluator** uses the Playwright MCP to click through the running app like a user, testing UI, API endpoints, and database state, then files bugs against the sprint contract.

**Sprint contracts:** Before coding each sprint, the generator proposes what it will build and how success will be verified. The evaluator reviews the proposal, and they iterate until they agree. The agents communicate through files. One contract had 27 criteria for the level editor.

**Grading criteria:**
- *Full-stack:* product depth, functionality, visual design, and code quality. Each has a hard threshold, and falling below any one fails the sprint.
- *Frontend:* design quality, originality, craft, and functionality. Design and originality were weighted more heavily, since Claude already handled craft and functionality well by default. The author calibrated the evaluator with few-shot examples and tuned its prompt, since out of the box it talked itself into approving flawed work.

**Context resets vs. compaction:** Resets clear the window and hand off structured state to a fresh agent, which gives a clean slate. Compaction summarizes history in place and keeps the same agent going, so it doesn't address "context anxiety." Sonnet 4.5 showed that anxiety strongly enough that resets were essential. Opus 4.5 largely removed the behavior, so the v2 harness dropped resets and relied on the SDK's automatic compaction.

**What worked:**
- The solo run on the retro game maker (20 min, $9) produced an app whose play mode didn't respond to input.
- The full harness (6 hr, $200) produced richer editors and a working built-in AI integration. It was playable, though physics and level-design issues remained.
- The frontend loop produced a creative pivot on the museum site's tenth iteration, which the author called a leap he hadn't seen from single-pass generation.

**What didn't:**
- Claude as a QA agent initially spotted real issues, then dismissed them. It also tested superficially.
- Without the planner, the generator under-scoped the work.
- The DAW's QA still found stubbed features, such as audio recording that only toggled a button.
- The agent couldn't judge musical taste, since Claude can't hear.

**Cost and time:**
- v2 DAW run: planner $0.46 (4.7 min); build round 1 $71.08 (2 hr 7 min); QA rounds totaled roughly $3 to $4 each. Total: $124.70, with the table listing 3 hr 50 min.
- The author noted the full harness cost over 20x the solo run.

**Lessons on removing components:**
- Each harness component encodes an assumption about what the model can't do alone. Those assumptions should be stress-tested, since they go stale as models improve.
- Removing one component at a time, rather than cutting radically, made it clearer which parts were load-bearing.
- With Opus 4.6, the sprint construct was removed, and the planner and evaluator were kept. The evaluator moved to a single end-of-run pass and was judged worth its cost mainly for tasks beyond what the model handles reliably solo.
- The author's conclusion: the space of interesting harness combinations "moves" as models improve rather than shrinking, so harnesses should be re-examined whenever a new model arrives.

**Free License team size limit**
- The Free License covers "an organization or team of individuals with up to 3 people."
- Single-person companies can also use it, "as long as your total headcount is 3 or less."
- For agencies working on client-owned projects, headcount is combined for the 4-person threshold.

**AI-generated Remotion code**
- Building a service that uses AI to generate and render Remotion code is permitted. Your customers don't need a Company License.
- End users may edit code that your service originally generated.
- Users may not upload their own Remotion code to your service for rendering.
- The FAQ also says that people who write Remotion code "themselves or using agentic coding tools" need a "Remotion for Creators" seat at $25/month per person.

**Prompt-to-video services**
- The FAQ states that organizations building "prompt-to-video tools, automated video pipelines or using the Remotion Player" fall under Remotion for Automators.
- That plan costs $0.01 per render, with a $100/month minimum.
- Automations are not covered by the Free License unless you are otherwise eligible for it. The FAQ says that if you are eligible, "you can also run an automation."

content.content:
**Workflows vs. agents**
- **Workflows:** "Workflows are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths." They offer predictability for well-defined tasks.
- **Agents:** LLMs direct their own processes and tool use, keeping control over how they finish a task. They suit open-ended problems where the number of steps can't be predicted in advance.

**Evaluator-optimizer pattern**
- One LLM call generates a response while another evaluates it and gives feedback, in a loop. It resembles a writer revising a draft.
- **When to use it:** when there are clear evaluation criteria and iteration adds measurable value. Good signs are that feedback demonstrably improves LLM output and that the LLM can produce useful critiques itself. Examples include literary translation and multi-round search tasks.

**Ground truth at each step**
- Agents need to check progress against the environment, such as tool results or code execution output, at every step. Pausing for human checkpoints and stopping conditions, like a maximum iteration count, help keep them under control.

**Tool design (agent-computer interface)**
- Tool definitions deserve as much prompt-engineering effort as the main prompt. Treat the agent-computer interface with the same care as a human-computer interface.
- Test tools by running many example inputs to find the model's mistakes, then iterate.
- Make tools hard to misuse ("poka-yoke"). In the SWE-bench work, requiring absolute file paths removed a recurring error. The team reportedly spent more time on tool optimization than on the overall prompt.

**Advice on simplicity**
- Begin with the simplest solution and add complexity only when needed. Consider adding it "only when it demonstrably improves outcomes."
- Start with direct LLM API calls rather than frameworks, since frameworks can hide prompts and responses and make debugging harder.
- Core agent principles are simplicity, transparency (showing planning steps), and careful tool documentation and testing.

content.content:
**Harness overview**

The article describes a two-part harness for long-running agents that work across many context windows.

- **Initializer agent:** Runs only on the first session. It uses a specialized prompt to set up the environment: an `init.sh` script, a progress log, and an initial git commit.
- **Coding agent:** Runs in every later session. It makes one piece of incremental progress and leaves the project in a tidy state for the next session. The article notes the two are separate only because of their different starting prompts; the system prompt, tools, and harness are otherwise the same.

**Feature list (JSON)**

The initializer expands the user's prompt into a detailed feature list. For a claude.ai clone, that was over 200 features, all initially marked failing. Each entry has a category, description, test steps, and a `passes` flag. Coding agents may only change `passes`. The authors chose JSON because models are less likely to improperly alter it than Markdown. They warn that "It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests because this could lead to missing or buggy functionality."

**Progress file and git**

A progress file (`claude-progress.txt`) logs what each session did. Together with git history, it lets a fresh agent quickly see the project's state. Agents are asked to "commit its progress to git with descriptive commit messages," which allows bad changes to be reverted and working states to be recovered.

**Testing with browser automation**

Agents often marked features complete after only unit tests or `curl` checks. Prompting them to use browser automation (the Puppeteer MCP server) and to "do all testing as a human user would" greatly improved end-to-end verification. A known limit is that Claude cannot see browser-native alert modals, so features that rely on them were buggier.

**Session startup routine**

Each coding session begins by checking the working directory, reading recent git logs and the progress file, and choosing the highest-priority unfinished feature. It then runs `init.sh` and a basic end-to-end test to catch any bugs left by the previous session before starting new work.

**Failure modes and fixes**

- **Trying to do too much at once:** The agent ran out of context mid-feature. *Fix:* a feature list, with one feature worked on per session.
- **Leaving undocumented, half-built work:** The next agent had to guess what happened. *Fix:* git commits, progress notes, and ending each session in a clean state.
- **Declaring victory too early:** Later agents saw some progress and called the job done. *Fix:* the complete feature list as the scope definition.
- **Marking features done without proper testing:** *Fix:* self-verification end-to-end before setting `passes` to true.
- **Wasting time working out how to run the app:** *Fix:* an `init.sh` script that starts the dev server.

content.content:
**Technical comparison (HyperFrames vs. Remotion), based only on the article**

| Dimension | HyperFrames | Remotion |
|---|---|---|
| **Determinism model** | Claims "deterministic local rendering," meaning the same output every time. The engine reads the DOM at a given state and captures it as a frame. | The article describes it as bridging React's asynchronous rendering with frame-by-frame video requirements, but makes no determinism claim. |
| **Lint / inspect / verification** | Not covered. | Not covered. |
| **Licensing** | Described as open-sourced by HeyGen, with a link to a GitHub repo labeled "Powered by HyperFrames OSS." No license name or terms are given. | Not addressed. |
| **Rendering speed** | No benchmarks. The article says a lighter approach "theoretically" has less to interpret and "could mean" faster local rendering and lower CPU overhead. | No benchmarks. The article notes it requires "a lot of under-the-hood heavy lifting." |
| **Authoring model** | Plain HTML, CSS, and data attributes; no React. | React and TypeScript. |
| **Limits and caveats** | None discussed for HyperFrames. | Tied to React; the article cites a large ecosystem and years of community troubleshooting as strengths. |

**Unverified marketing claims**

- That HyperFrames is "agent-native" and that LLMs write its HTML "reliably" and "rarely" make mistakes. No evidence is provided.
- That AI agents avoid "hallucinating a dozen missing dependencies" with HyperFrames but not with Remotion.
- That output is "pixel-perfect" and deterministic in practice.
- That rendering is "lighter," faster, and lower in CPU overhead, including at "thousands of concurrent" requests. None of this is measured.
- That HyperFrames is a "shortcut" for AI-first products. This comes from the vendor's own blog, which promotes its product.

The search turned up the Huang et al. paper and several secondary summaries. It did not return material on Reflexion or on verifier-based setups, so those parts of your query aren't covered.

**The paper:** Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet is by Jie Huang and six co-authors from Google DeepMind and UIUC. It was accepted to ICLR 2024 and first posted to arXiv as 2310.01798 in October 2023. Its focus is intrinsic self-correction, where an LLM tries to fix its initial responses using only its own capabilities, without external feedback.

**Main findings:** The authors report that, for reasoning tasks, LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times their performance even degrades after self-correction. A summary of the paper says that prior claims of self-correction gains often stem from using oracle labels, leading to an unfair comparison, or from suboptimal initial prompt design. It also finds that multi-agent debate, when compared with an equivalent number of responses, does not outperform self-consistency.

**Relevance to your Reflexion / Self-Refine / verifier question:** A blog post on the paper describes it as the direct counterpoint to the CRITIC and Reflexion lines of work. Another post lists Self-Refine as the primary paper that Huang et al. critique. The post also says CRITIC's tool-grounded critiquing genuinely helped. Beyond these mentions, the results don't describe Reflexion's or Self-Refine's methods, and they don't cover verifier-based results in detail. For primary details on those, check the original Self-Refine (NeurIPS 2023) and Reflexion papers directly.

**Verification commands (`lint`, `inspect`, `check`, `snapshot`):** The page doesn't say what these verify. It lists them only in passing. The `/hyperframes-cli` skill covers "`init`, `lint`, `check`, `snapshot`, `preview`, `render`, `publish`, `doctor`," and the stack table describes the CLI as able to "lint, inspect, and render local video projects." Nothing on the page mentions layout overflow, contrast, determinism, or missing-asset checks.

**TTS / voice:** The page doesn't specify this. Narration is mentioned only generally. The `/media-use` skill can resolve a voice need by generating it "via TTS/music/image models when the catalog misses," but the page names no provider, doesn't say whether generation runs locally or in the cloud, and doesn't mention API keys.

**Known limitations:** The page has no limitations section. These are the closest items:
- The Studio browser editor is marked "Available, evolving."
- Skills installed through `skills add` may trail `main`, since the registry "can lag `main` by hours." `npx hyperframes skills update` pulls from `main` directly.
- The full repo clone needs Git LFS for about 240 MB of golden regression `.mp4` files, or you can skip them with `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1`.
- The interactive skills picker doesn't run in non-interactive mode, where omitting `--skill` installs all 21 skills.
- AWS Lambda rendering is marked "Available," but the page doesn't state how mature it is.

## 1b. Research (10 Oct 2026): what exists, what it teaches, what it changes

Read from primary pages where I could; claims marked "unverified" come only from a vendor or a blog. Nothing here was run yet.

### Open-source video harnesses and renderers

| Project | What it is | Licence | Fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [HyperFrames](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes) (HeyGen) | "Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents." HTML + CSS + seekable animations (GSAP, CSS, Lottie, Three.js, WAAPI), headless Chrome frame capture, FFmpeg encode, audio mixing with VO ducking. CLI `init/preview/lint/inspect/check/snapshot/render`; 21 agent skills (Claude Code plugin). Node 22+ and FFmpeg. About 60k stars on the repo page | Apache-2.0, no per-render fees | **Same model as our `video/launch`** (seek the page, screenshot each frame, pipe to ffmpeg). Best candidate to adopt as the render layer. What `lint`/`inspect` check is not stated on the README; determinism "same input, same frames" is the project's own claim, unverified by us |
| [Remotion](https://www.remotion.dev/docs/license/faq) | React/TypeScript, incumbent; official agent skills | Source-available: free for up to 3 people (we are 1), automated pipelines and prompt-to-video products fall under "Automators" ($0.01 per render, $100/month minimum); building a service that generates Remotion code with AI is allowed | Works, but a React build step for little gain, and a licence clause that matters if Storybound sells the video feature |
| [Revideo](https://github.com/redotvideo/revideo) | TypeScript, headless `renderVideo()`, audio export, serverless; 4.1k stars | MIT | Good for imperative animation; no agent tooling; maintenance date not visible on the page |
| Motion Canvas | Generator-function animation editor (Revideo's origin) | MIT | Hand-authored animations, not an agent target |
| [OpenEdit](https://github.com/veedstudio/open-edit) (VEED) | A skill: agent transcribes (WhisperX), composes an HTML page, renders frame by frame in a browser, **reviews the frames**, re-renders only what changed; no GUI | Apache-2.0 | Closest in spirit. Its verification is "the agent looks at frames"; the README says "expect rough edges". 25 commits, young |
| [agent-video-studio](https://github.com/mikolajmikolajczak0108/agent-video-studio) | JSON **reviewable edit plans**, FFmpeg/Whisper scripts, **export QC** (duration, frame timing, audio, colour, decoding); "the agent plans and reviews; the scripts execute explicit operations" | MIT | Right division of labour and the right kind of deterministic QC; but 0 stars and 3 commits, so a pattern to copy, not a dependency |
| edit-ai, WeftCut, OpenChatCut | Agents driving a timeline editor through MCP tools (16 and more tools; approval before destructive actions); OpenChatCut is AGPL | MIT / AGPL | A GUI timeline is the wrong target: we want deterministic code from a spec |

Result of the survey: **the renderer problem is solved and open**; I found no open-source harness (from the pages I read) that checks every number on screen against a source of truth, runs per-promise verification with repair, and ships a receipt. HyperFrames' `lint`/`inspect` and agent-video-studio's QC cover technical correctness only. That gap is our contribution and it is the same idea as the oath.

### What the agent-loop literature and engineering posts say (and where we already agree)

| Source | Finding | What we do with it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anthropic, [Harness design for long-running application development](https://anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps) | Planner / generator / **separate evaluator** that drives the live output (Playwright) and files bugs against a shared definition of done (a "sprint contract"); out of the box the evaluator "talked itself into approving flawed work" and had to be calibrated with few-shot examples; the full harness cost about 20x the solo run ($200 vs $9) but produced working output the solo run did not; every harness component encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do alone, so re-test it when the model changes | Our judge is already a separate model (K2) from the writer (Gemini). The video oath is the contract, written before rendering. Keep the evaluator, drop anything that cannot show it changes the outcome; log cost of the loop honestly (B1 vs B0 does this for stories) |
| Anthropic, [Effective harnesses for long-running agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents) | JSON feature list the agent may only flip `passes` on (JSON because models alter it less than Markdown); progress file + git commits so a fresh session recovers state; end each session clean; agents "declared victory early" and marked features done without end-to-end tests until told to test as a human would | The spec and the oath are JSON; promises have a status the repair loop may change but never delete. `hackathon.md` and the ledger are our progress file. Verify through the rendered output (frames, audio), not the spec |
| Anthropic, [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) | Workflows (predefined code paths) vs agents (LLM directs its own steps); **evaluator-optimizer** fits when criteria are clear; agents need ground truth from the environment at each step and a maximum iteration count; invest in tool design and make tools hard to misuse; start simple, no framework you cannot debug | Our video pipeline is a **workflow with one agentic loop** (verify then repair, max 2 attempts), not a free-roaming agent: video promises are clear and checkable. Tools validate at the boundary (a `claim` block cannot hold a literal number) |
| Huang et al., [LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798) (ICLR 2024) | Without external feedback, self-correction often does not help and can hurt | Matches our own measurement so far: B2 (same model reviews its own story) ships a broken promise in about 90% of stories, B1 (external judge + deterministic checks) in 0 of 12 at the interim. Put B2 vs B1 in the video story, with the numbers from the final sweep |
| [Agentic Video Generation: text to executable event graphs via tool-constrained LLM planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10383) | A staged flagship-model pipeline produced 0 executable specs in 50 attempts; agents acting only through tools that check operations against simulator state produced valid specs 20 of 25 (80%) on a budget model; evaluated by round-trip reconstruction | Strongest support for "validate at the tool boundary". We borrow the idea (claim blocks resolve against evidence at write time) but not the simulator |
| [VideoAgent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10076) (NeurIPS 2025) and VISTA (arXiv 2510.15831) | VLM as the reward/critic that selects or refines generated video plans | Supports the judged frame checks (legible, matches narration); these papers are about generative video, not deterministic render, so the evidence is indirect |

### What this changes in the plan

1. **Do not write a renderer from scratch.** Time-boxed spike (45 minutes, Sat evening): render two scenes of `scenes.json` with HyperFrames on this Windows machine (Node 24, ffmpeg present), compare frame-exactness across two runs (hash the frames), and read what `lint`/`inspect` catch. If it works, adopt it for render, audio mix and layout lint, and keep only our layers on top (spec, claim resolution, oath checks, repair, receipt, tracing). If it does not, keep `video/launch/render.mjs` (already works, ~100 lines) and add what is missing. Decision recorded in `hackathon.md` with the evidence either way.
2. **Our part is the verifier.** The differentiated work is `claims_sourced`, `claims_match_ledger`, `tools_covered`, `no_child_data`, `no_secrets` and the receipt: none of the projects above ship these.
3. **Keep the loop small** (Anthropic's own advice): workflow with one verify-repair loop, max 2 attempts, JSON spec/oath the repair step cannot delete from, external evaluator for judged checks. Measure the loop's cost against a no-verify run (B0-style arm for video) so the harness is itself an experiment with numbers.
4. **Licence**: HyperFrames Apache-2.0 and Revideo MIT are safe if the video export ships as a product feature; Remotion's Automators clause is a cost line for cfo.ai if we used it. Another reason to prefer HyperFrames.
5. **Honest caveats to carry into the submission**: HyperFrames' determinism and agent-friendliness claims come from its authors and blogs; the Anthropic cost figures are one project's; the self-correction paper is about reasoning, not video.

## 2. What exists and what is wrong with it

+Result of the survey: **the renderer problem is solved and open**; I found no open-source harness (from the pages I read) that checks every number on screen against a source of truth, runs per-promise verification with repair, and ships a receipt. HyperFrames' `lint`/`inspect` and agent-video-studio's QC cover technical correctness only. That gap is our contribution and it is the same idea as the oath.
+### What the agent-loop literature and engineering posts say (and where we already agree)
+| Source | Finding | What we do with it |

+| Anthropic, [Harness design for long-running application development](https://anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps) | Planner / generator / **separate evaluator** that drives the live output (Playwright) and files bugs against a shared definition of done (a "sprint contract"); out of the box the evaluator "talked itself into approving flawed work" and had to be calibrated with few-shot examples; the full harness cost about 20x the solo run ($200 vs $9) but produced working output the solo run did not; every harness component encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do alone, so re-test it when the model changes | Our judge is already a separate model (K2) from the writer (Gemini). The video oath is the contract, written before rendering. Keep the evaluator, drop anything that cannot show it changes the outcome; log cost of the loop honestly (B1 vs B0 does this for stories) |

+| Anthropic, [Effective harnesses for long-running agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents) | JSON feature list the agent may only flip `passes` on (JSON because models alter it less than Markdown); progress file + git commits so a fresh session recovers state; end each session clean; agents "declared victory early" and marked features done without end-to-end tests until told to test as a human would | The spec and the oath are JSON; promises have a status the repair loop may change but never delete. `hackathon.md` and the ledger are our progress file. Verify through the rendered output (frames, audio), not the spec |

+| Anthropic, [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) | Workflows (predefined code paths) vs agents (LLM directs its own steps); **evaluator-optimizer** fits when criteria are clear; agents need ground truth from the environment at each step and a maximum iteration count; invest in tool design and make tools hard to misuse; start simple, no framework you cannot debug | Our video pipeline is a **workflow with one agentic loop** (verify then repair, max 2 attempts), not a free-roaming agent: video promises are clear and checkable. Tools validate at the boundary (a `claim` block cannot hold a literal number) |

+| Huang et al., [LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798) (ICLR 2024) | Without external feedback, self-correction often does not help and can hurt | Matches our own measurement so far: B2 (same model reviews its own story) ships a broken promise in about 90% of stories, B1 (external judge + deterministic checks) in 0 of 12 at the interim. Put B2 vs B1 in the video story, with the numbers from the final sweep |

+| [Agentic Video Generation: text to executable event graphs via tool-constrained LLM planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10383) | A staged flagship-model pipeline produced 0 executable specs in 50 attempts; agents acting only through tools that check operations against simulator state produced valid specs 20 of 25 (80%) on a budget model; evaluated by round-trip reconstruction | Strongest support for "validate at the tool boundary". We borrow the idea (claim blocks resolve against evidence at write time) but not the simulator |

+| [VideoAgent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10076) (NeurIPS 2025) and VISTA (arXiv 2510.15831) | VLM as the reward/critic that selects or refines generated video plans | Supports the judged frame checks (legible, matches narration); these papers are about generative video, not deterministic render, so the evidence is indirect |
+### What this changes in the plan

+1. **Do not write a renderer from scratch.** Time-boxed spike (45 minutes, Sat evening): render two scenes of `scenes.json` with HyperFrames on this Windows machine (Node 24, ffmpeg present), compare frame-exactness across two runs (hash the frames), and read what `lint`/`inspect` catch. If it works, adopt it for render, audio mix and layout lint, and keep only our layers on top (spec, claim resolution, oath checks, repair, receipt, tracing). If it does not, keep `video/launch/render.mjs` (already works, ~100 lines) and add what is missing. Decision recorded in `hackathon.md` with the evidence either way.

+2. **Our part is the verifier.** The differentiated work is `claims_sourced`, `claims_match_ledger`, `tools_covered`, `no_child_data`, `no_secrets` and the receipt: none of the projects above ship these.

+3. **Keep the loop small** (Anthropic's own advice): workflow with one verify-repair loop, max 2 attempts, JSON spec/oath the repair step cannot delete from, external evaluator for judged checks. Measure the loop's cost against a no-verify run (B0-style arm for video) so the harness is itself an experiment with numbers.

+4. **Licence**: HyperFrames Apache-2.0 and Revideo MIT are safe if the video export ships as a product feature; Remotion's Automators clause is a cost line for cfo.ai if we used it. Another reason to prefer HyperFrames.

+5. **Honest caveats to carry into the submission**: HyperFrames' determinism and agent-friendliness claims come from its authors and blogs; the Anthropic cost figures are one project's; the self-correction paper is about reasoning, not video.
## 2. What exists and what is wrong with it
| Today (`video/launch/`) | Problem for a harness |

content.text:
Open-source video harnesses do exist, and the renderer side is already solved. I added the findings to [docs/planning/video-harness.md](docs/planning/video-harness.md) (section 1b) and changed the plan to match. I haven't run any of these tools yet, and nothing is committed. Sweep 2 is still running.

**Video harnesses and renderers:**
- **HyperFrames** (HeyGen, Apache-2.0) uses the same approach as `video/launch`: seekable HTML, headless Chrome frames, ffmpeg. It also has a CLI (`lint`, `inspect`, `render`), audio mixing and Claude Code skills. It needs Node 22+, and this machine has Node 24 and ffmpeg. The README doesn't say what `lint` and `inspect` check. Its determinism claim comes from the project itself, so I haven't confirmed it.
- **Remotion** is free for teams of up to 3 (we're 1). The "Automators" tier at $0.01 per render, $100/month minimum would apply if Storybound sold the video feature.
- **Revideo** (MIT) has headless rendering and audio but no agent tooling.
- **OpenEdit** (Apache-2.0) is the closest in spirit: the agent composes HTML, renders, and looks at the frames. Its README says to "expect rough edges".
- **agent-video-studio** (MIT) has JSON edit plans and technical export checks, which is the right pattern. It has 0 stars and 3 commits, so it's something to copy, not depend on.
- The timeline-editor projects (edit-ai, WeftCut, OpenChatCut) are the wrong target. We want video generated from a spec, not a GUI editor.
- **The gap:** from the pages I read, none checks that every number on screen matches a source file, runs repair per promise, or ships a receipt. That checking layer is what we'd build.

**What the agent-loop research says, and what we do with it:**
- **Anthropic's harness posts:**
  - Use a separate evaluator, which fits our Gemini writer and K2 judge. In their run the evaluator had to be calibrated because it kept approving flawed work.
  - Keep the spec as JSON the repair step can't delete from.
  - The full harness cost about 20x the solo run, so the video loop's cost must be measured against a no-verify arm.
- **Huang et al., ICLR 2024:** self-correction without external feedback often doesn't help. Our sweep matches this so far: B2, where the model reviews its own story, ships a broken promise in about 90% of stories. B1 shipped 0 of 12 in the partial data, and the final sweep numbers will replace those.
- **Arxiv 2604.10383:** a staged pipeline produced 0 valid specs in 50 attempts, and agents limited to tools that validate their inputs produced valid ones 80% of the time. We borrow the idea. A claim block can't hold a typed number; it resolves from an evidence file.

**Changes to the plan:**
- Don't write a renderer from scratch. A 45-minute HyperFrames spike on Saturday evening renders two scenes twice and compares the frames. If it works, we adopt it and build only the verifier, repair loop and receipt on top. If not, we keep `render.mjs`.
- The video pipeline stays a fixed workflow with one verify-and-repair loop, capped at 2 attempts, not a free-roaming agent.

**Blockers and decisions:**
- **neatlogs:** the MCP rejected the API key at startup (HTTP 401), so I can't check traces in the dashboard until the key is fixed. If it was rotated, the new one needs to go into the MCP config.
- **Entire:** there are still 0 checkpoints. The first commit made in this repo should produce one.
- **Submission link:** the repo is private, so the Entire checkpoint link only works for judges if the repo is public or they have access.
- **Child's drawings:** the launch video uses a child's drawings and cutout images. They need a parent's consent and no visible face before publishing.

Sources:
- [HyperFrames](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes)
- [Remotion license FAQ](https://www.remotion.dev/docs/license/faq)
- [Revideo](https://github.com/redotvideo/revideo)
- [OpenEdit](https://github.com/veedstudio/open-edit)
- [agent-video-studio](https://github.com/mikolajmikolajczak0108/agent-video-studio)
- [Anthropic: harness design](https://anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps)
- [Anthropic: effective harnesses](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)
- [Anthropic: building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Huang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798)
- [Agentic video generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10383)
- [VideoAgent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10076)

@pytest.mark.parametrize("age", [4, 5, 6, 7, 8])
def test_writer_prompts_state_the_reading_limit_the_verifier_enforces(age):
    """HR-001: the writer is told the same per-age sentence limit that age_reading_level checks."""
    from storybound import prompts
    from storybound.oath.deterministic import max_sentence_words

    n = max_sentence_words(age)
    for system in (prompts.WRITE_SYSTEM, prompts.BASELINE_SYSTEM):
        assert f"at most {n} words" in system.format(age=age, max_words=n)
E
head -12 tests/test_oath.py | grep -n "import pytest" ; .venv/Scripts/python.exe -m pytest tests -q 2>&1 | tail -4
